assumptions: Function estimation is sufficient for successful goal inference.
Locally-linear learning captures the essential dynamics of interaction.
Interaction histories contain implicit objective signals sufficient for convergence.
definition.falsification: Agents consistently fail to converge to stable objective-like functions across diverse interaction datasets, showing no objective-like persistence.
definition.statement: Autonomous systems utilizing locally-linear learning formulations for function estimation can successfully derive coherent, persistent objectives from interaction histories.
definition.uncertainty: The length of interaction required to stabilize an objective and the impact of initial noise remain unknown.

proposal.summary: Proposing a revised hypothesis for autonomous objective formation under the selected topic using locally-linear learning formulations.
proposal.title: Autonomous Objective Formulation Hypothesis Revision

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=epistemic+return+on+investment+diminishing+returns+research+agenda+abandonment+decision+criteria&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.1078502\", \"title\": [\"Social Discounting with Diminishing Returns on Investment\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>I estimate the social discount rate allowing returns on investment to differ from returns on wealth.  Historical returns on wealth and investment in the United States imply estimates of pure time preference and risk aversion, which I use to project returns going forward.    I generalize the Ramsey Rule for optimal investment to account for any difference between rates of return on wealth and investment.  Empirically, the rate of return on investment is below that on wealth, and both are declining, so drawing the distinction implies less investment as a fraction of income than under the original Ramsey Rule.  The analysis suggests pure time preference of 1.02%, a descriptive social discount rate of 7.35%, and a prescriptive rate of 6.33%, based on my interpretation of the Biblical Golden Rule: zero pure time preference.  This also implies an increase in investment over historical and projected rates of about 4% of GDP.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1078502\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2007]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1515/9783110329216.39\", \"title\": [\"Chapter 4: Diminishing Returns\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110329216.39\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013, 12, 31]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.1478564\", \"title\": [\"Diminishing Returns to Investment Vis-À-Vis Firm Age\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>To the extent that firm information provides data to complete markets, firm characteristics determine value to investors.  Contrarily, investors are motivated by prospect theory to bid up firm prices without information especially concerning diminishing returns to investments. The valuation effect of investments is highly subjective in the case of R&D (growth options) and more concrete in regards to capital expenditures (assets-in-place).  This study contributes to the investment knowledge frontier by analyzing diminishing returns to research and development (R&D) and capital expenditures in regards to a firm’s age.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1478564\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6737161\", \"title\": [\"Diminishing Returns to Road Investment: Evidence from Cost-Benefit Analyses\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>We study long-run trends in the economic returns to Norwegian road investments using a harmonised dataset of 360 ex ante cost-benefit analyses from 1974 to 2024. Projects are drawn from official planning documents and adjusted for changes in appraisal parameters and construction cost inflation. Using the net benefit-cost ratio (NBCR) as our measure of economic return, we find a significant negative time trend in NBCR that remains after conditioning on observed project characteristics. When investment costs are deflated with the construction cost index and appraisal parameters harmonised, the trend remains negative and is possibly hump-shaped. We further show that the decline in economic return is associated with lower travel-time savings, consistent with diminishing returns in a mature road network. By contrast, the decline does not appear to be driven by increasing project size or by shifts towards projects with a larger share of costly components, such as tunnels and bridges.
